podcast.body: Written by Tom York during a drinking binge at university, reflecting his unrequited love for a girl he often saw in Oxford cafes and bars over eight months. Tom initially hid the song, considering it "too weak and wimpy," but when presented to the band, Johnny Greenwood vehemently disliked it, attempting to sabotage the studio recording by inserting a loud, grinding scratch with his guitar just before the chorus. Unbeknownst to the band, the producer secretly recorded this raw take, which became the version released to the public. The original version contained an "F-bomb" which was later reluctantly changed to "very" for release to gain airplay. The song was later subject to a copyright infringement lawsuit by The Hollies, who claimed it was too similar to their 1972 song "The Air That I Breathe." As a result, Albert Hammond Sr. and Mike Hazelwood now each receive 25% of the writing credit. Released as a single on September 21, 1992, with 6,000 copies pressed, it initially reached number 78 on the charts and was played only twice by the BBC before being pulled for being "too depressing." However, it gained massive popularity in Israel after an EMI employee, Uzi Price, gave it to DJ Yoav Kutner of Israeli Armed Forces Radio. Its success in Israel prompted EMI to interrupt Radiohead's UK tour for three shows in Tel Aviv in March/April 1993, further boosting its hit status. An Israeli import later led to play on a San Francisco radio station, and subsequently across North America, becoming one of the biggest alternative singles globally and a top 40 hit in some countries. Tom York used the song's earnings to buy a house, which he named "the house that Creep built." It is now considered one of the three great slacker anthems of the early 90s, alongside Nirvana's "Smells Like Teen Spirit" and Beck's "Loser." "The Creepe Pee was released on September 21st, 1992."
